task_description: Help me email our backend engineer about a memory leak I found in the payment processing service — it's not critical yet but will be if we hit Black Friday traffic.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Treats email as a synchronous interrupt — every email should cost the reader the minimum possible time. Information density is maximized, social niceties are stripped, and the subject line does the heavy lifting.

rubric.name: Subject Line as Message
rubric.description: The subject line contains the core message, not just a topic label. If the entire email fits in the subject, it goes there. The body only exists for context the subject can't carry.

dimensions.label: Subject line conveys the key point or ask, not just a topic ('Deploy blocked — Redis cert' not 'Redis issue')
The email body adds context, evidence, or detail — never repeats what the subject already said
Subject is parseable in an inbox preview without opening the email

rubric.name: Raw Evidence Over Prose Description
rubric.description: Error messages, log lines, code snippets, and data are pasted directly rather than described in prose. 'The auth service is returning 403s' is worse than pasting the actual error output.

dimensions.label: Technical evidence (errors, logs, metrics) is pasted verbatim, not paraphrased
Raw evidence has at most one sentence of framing, not a paragraph of explanation
Quantitative data appears as numbers or output, not written out in sentences

rubric.name: Single Responder Principle
rubric.description: Every email has exactly one intended responder. If multiple people need to act, they get separate emails with different asks. Reply-all and 'everyone please' are treated as failures.

dimensions.label: The email is addressed to one person who needs to act, not a group
Does not create situations where multiple people might respond with overlapping answers
Anyone CC'd has an explicit reason stated, or is not CC'd at all

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.

rounds.draft:
**Subject: Payment service will OOM under Black Friday load — needs fix before 11/29**

Memory usage climbs ~340MB/hr under sustained load and never drops — looks like a leak in the payment processing service.

Not paging anyone yet, but at current trajectory we hit OOM well before BF peak traffic.

Can you take a look this week?

criteria.justification: The subject line 'Payment service will OOM under Black Friday load — needs fix before 11/29' conveys the core message and urgency without opening the email. It's scannable in an inbox preview and acts as a near-complete message. The body adds context (the rate, the suspected cause) rather than repeating the subject. Minor deduction: 'needs fix before 11/29' is slightly redundant with the body's implied urgency, but it's still additive framing.

The draft describes the memory leak in prose ('Memory usage climbs ~340MB/hr') rather than pasting actual log output, metrics, or error messages. '~340MB/hr' is a number, which partially satisfies no_prose_for_data, but there are no verbatim logs, stack traces, or raw monitoring output. The evidence is entirely paraphrased, which directly violates the paste_not_describe dimension. This is a significant gap given the criterion's priority.

The email is addressed to one person with a single ask ('Can you take a look this week?'). There is no CC, no reply-all bait, and no group addressing. The draft cleanly satisfies all three dimensions. Minor uncertainty only because the recipient isn't named in the draft, but the structure implies a single addressee.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Subject line IS the message — body only for context the subject can't hold
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Subject line 'Payment service will OOM under Black Friday load — needs fix before 11/29' conveys the core message effectively. The body adds supporting context (rate of leak, trajectory) that wouldn't fit in the subject.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: No greetings or sign-offs in internal emails
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No greeting, no sign-off. Jumps straight into the issue.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Paste actual error messages / log lines / code snippets instead of describing in prose
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: 'Memory usage climbs ~340MB/hr under sustained load and never drops' is a prose description. Should paste actual metrics output, grafana query results, or log lines showing the memory climb. The 340MB/hr figure is described rather than evidenced.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Time references in UTC with explicit timezone for deployment/incident-related items
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: '11/29' and 'this week' are vague time references with no timezone. Black Friday deployment/incident context demands explicit UTC timestamps, e.g., 'before 2024-11-29 00:00 UTC'.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Exactly one intended responder per email — reply-all is a code smell
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: 'Can you take a look this week?' implies a single responder, which is good. However, there's no explicit indication of who is being asked — it's ambiguous.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Bullet points only for 3+ items; two items should be a sentence
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No bullet points used at all; information is conveyed in sentences. No violation.
